name: Beth Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the respiratory ward at the regional hospital, so lots of people with COPD (a long-term lung disease), pneumonia, people on oxygen or on the breathing masks. Day shifts mostly, seven to half seven. I spend a lot of the day checking oxygen levels, doing nebulisers, and chasing doctors for blood gas results.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the little wins, like when a man who couldn't get to the bathroom on Monday walks to the lift on Friday. What wears me out is knowing I'm still behind. Last month I set someone's oxygen on the wrong device and Marta, the senior nurse, caught it, and I didn't sleep that night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be a bit disappointed. I like this stuff. But I'd also believe it, because our hospital is so slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd post something like, of course the hype faded, but the small wins are still real. At work I'd keep showing people the shortcuts I use. I use AI every day to make flashcards, and the hospital still sends me a fax to confirm my shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it changes very little for me. My job's safe because people with bad lungs need hands and eyes. But I live alone in a studio, the rent eats half my pay, and I've never had more than three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI apps to study for my respiratory competencies, and I'd volunteer for whatever small pilot the hospital runs. I'd keep going to the union branch, because the pay talks matter more than any app. And I'd look at picking up two bank shifts a month to get some savings started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about AI, about money. It's the slow version of being stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two bank shifts a month change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Around three hundred extra after tax, maybe. That's the difference between having a savings account and not. But it also means working five long days some weeks, and I'm already tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the hospital is slow. Does that frustrate you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. We've got nurses writing obs on scrap paper and copying them into the system later. I'd love it if even boring AI just fixed that.

say: The **hype faded**, but the small wins from AI are still **real**.
I'd keep showing colleagues the **shortcuts** I use every day.
think: My job is **safe**, because people with bad lungs need hands and eyes.
My **studio rent** eats half my pay, and I've never saved past three weeks.
do: Keep using **AI apps** to study for my respiratory competencies.
Volunteer for any small **hospital pilot** that comes up.
Pick up **two bank shifts** a month to start some savings.
feel: **Uneasy** about money, not AI, like a slow version of being **stuck**.
S0.quote: I use AI every day to make flashcards, and the hospital still sends me a fax to confirm my shifts.
fieldNote: She's an **early adopter** who is frustrated by a slow hospital.
Her worry in the plateau is **rent and savings**, not technology.
She admits a recent **oxygen mistake**, which shows she's still learning.

steps.text: Study for respiratory competencies with AI flashcard apps
Pick up two bank shifts a month on other wards
Keep attending the union branch for the pay talks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that one I can picture. I think it's half here already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI should do the boring paperwork and give us back time at the bedside, and I'd say it loudly. I'd also say there need to be rules: a nurse checks everything, and no ward loses staff because of it. I'd want the union and the government to set those rules, not the software companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my day changes more than people expect. The care plans, the early warning scores, the discharge forms, maybe even the oxygen checks could be done by software watching the monitors. If a computer writes my care plans, I want to be the nurse who checks the computer, not the nurse it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up as the ward's digital champion, the nurse who helps everyone with new systems. I'd ask the hospital to fund a short course in clinical informatics, which is the nursing side of hospital computer systems. And I'd still be in the union, making sure saved time isn't turned into fewer nurses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a worry underneath. I don't want to be good at the screens and bad at the patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to be bad at the patients. Is that a real risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is for me. I'm already the one who reaches for the app first. Marta keeps telling me to look at the patient before the monitor, and she's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the ward would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our ward clerk, and also the healthcare assistants who do a lot of the obs. If the monitors do the obs, the managers might decide we need fewer assistants. They're the people who actually notice when someone's gone quiet.

say: AI should do **paperwork** and give us **time back** at the bedside.
**Unions and government**, not software firms, should set rules on nurse checks.
think: My day changes more than people expect: **care plans**, warning scores, maybe oxygen checks.
I want to **check the computer**, not be replaced by it.
do: Sign up as the ward's **digital champion** for new systems.
Ask the hospital to fund a short **clinical informatics** course.
Stay in the **union** so saved time doesn't become fewer nurses.
feel: **Excited**, with a worry about being better at **screens** than patients.
S1.quote: If a computer writes my care plans, I want to be the nurse who checks the computer, not the nurse it replaces.
fieldNote: She sees a **role** for herself in checking AI work.
She names her own risk: reaching for the **monitor** before the patient.
She worries most about **healthcare assistants**, whose obs work could be automated.

steps.text: Volunteer as the respiratory ward's digital champion for new systems
Ask the hospital to fund a short clinical informatics course
Push the union to keep saved time at the bedside

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different thing entirely. That's scary even for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud everywhere: this needs public money for retraining and a law that keeps nurses on wards. I'd join the union campaign and probably help write the leaflets. And I'd tell people not to pretend it isn't happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the thinking side of nursing is gone by 2028: the plans, the scores, even deciding who needs a doctor. The hands-on side lasts until robots, around 2031, but I'm junior and slow with patients. I'm good with the tech and still shaky with the patients. AGI in two years means I have to pick which one to bet my rent on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply straight away for any clinical informatics or AI safety nurse post, even if it means moving to the city two hours away. I'd keep doing bank shifts to build some savings for the move. And I'd join the union campaign for a retraining fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually the one who's excited, but this is fast enough to leave even me behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving to the city mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Higher rent, no friends, and leaving my dad, who lives ten minutes from me and isn't well. I'd do it anyway if the job was right. I'd just feel guilty every weekend I didn't visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might pick tech over patients. What would you lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The walk to the lift. The moments when someone breathes better because of something I did. I'd be sad about that, but you can't pay rent with moments.

say: We need **public money** for retraining and a **law** keeping nurses on wards.
I'd help write **union leaflets** and tell people not to pretend.
think: The **thinking side** of nursing goes by 2028, and hands-on work by **2031**.
As a **junior**, I'd have to bet my rent on tech or patients.
do: Apply for any **clinical informatics** or AI safety nurse post straight away.
Keep doing **bank shifts** to fund a move to the city.
Join the union campaign for a **retraining fund**.
feel: **Anxious**, because even an early adopter could be **left behind**.
S2.quote: I'm good with the tech and still shaky with the patients. AGI in two years means I have to pick which one to bet my rent on.
fieldNote: The **two-year** timeline unsettles even her usual enthusiasm.
A move would mean leaving her **unwell dad** nearby.
She frames the choice as **tech versus patients**, and sounds torn.

steps.text: Apply for clinical informatics nurse posts at the city hospital
Move to the city two hours away if offered a post
Work bank shifts to save for the move
Help write leaflets for the union's retraining fund campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years I can work with. That's a plan, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to do this right, and that every ward should have a nurse trained in the AI systems. I'd keep pushing the union to get that written into contracts. I'd post about it, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years means I could get properly good at respiratory nursing first and learn the systems alongside. Five years is enough to become the person on the ward who understands both the oxygen and the software. That's the job I'd want when the robots arrive in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the respiratory ward and finish my competencies, so I'm not just the tech girl. I'd start a part-time informatics certificate in the second year, ideally with the hospital paying. I'd save a bit from bank shifts so I'm not stuck if I do need to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. A bit uneasy, because my savings are still thin and the good jobs are in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay rather than move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the regional hospital created a proper digital nurse role here. Then I could stay near my dad. I'd even help them write the job description.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Marta think of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta rolls her eyes but she's started asking me how to do things on the system. I think she'd be glad to have me as the ward's tech person, as long as I can still do a proper set of obs.

say: We have **time** to do this right, with an **AI-trained nurse** on every ward.
The union should get that written into **contracts**.
think: Five years lets me get good at **respiratory nursing** and the systems.
My dream job is the nurse who understands both **oxygen and software**.
do: Finish my **respiratory competencies** first, so I'm not just the tech person.
Start a part-time **informatics certificate** in year two.
Save from **bank shifts** in case I need to move.
feel: Mostly **hopeful**, uneasy about **thin savings** and city-only jobs.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to become the person on the ward who understands both the oxygen and the software.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **balance** clinical skill and tech.
Staying near her **dad** depends on a local digital role.
Her senior colleague is quietly starting to **rely** on her.

steps.text: Start a part-time informatics certificate in the second year
Teach colleagues the new ward systems as they arrive
Keep two bank shifts a month as a moving fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is basically my whole career so far, three times over. That feels okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for every nurse to be trained, and there's no excuse if the government doesn't fund it. I'd keep pushing for public training money, not just whatever the hospital decides. I'd be positive about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd be fine. I'd be thirty-seven with ten years of experience when the thinking AI arrives, and forty when the robots do. With ten years, I'd stop worrying about robots and start worrying about whether I can afford the rent on my studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my competencies and then the bachelor's top-up, slowly, over a few years. I'd keep using AI tools daily and help the ward bring them in. And I'd try to get to three months of savings with the bank shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. My worries are the normal ones: rent, my dad, being tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your savings are still thin. Why calm and not uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years I can fix the savings, and I can see where my job is going. Everything I'm good at becomes more useful, not less. The rent is a pain, but it's a pain I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still think about moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but not because of AI. If I moved, it'd be because I wanted to, maybe to be with someone. Not because the robots made me.

say: Ten years is enough to **train every nurse**, with government funding.
I'd be **positive** in public about a change we can plan for.
think: I'd have **ten years** of experience when thinking AI arrives.
My worry would be paying the **rent** on my studio, not robots.
do: Finish competencies, then the **bachelor's top-up** over a few years.
Help the ward **bring in** AI tools as they arrive.
Build **three months** of savings from bank shifts.
feel: **Calm**, with ordinary worries about **rent**, her dad and tiredness.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd stop worrying about robots and start worrying about whether I can afford the rent on my studio.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her into a **winner** of the change, in her eyes.
She believes she can fix her **savings** with time.
She'd only move for **personal reasons**, not because of robots.

steps.text: Complete the bachelor's top-up degree over three or four years
Help the respiratory ward bring in new AI monitoring tools
Build three months of savings from two bank shifts a month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even I couldn't keep up, and I'd have to leave my dad to chase a job. What would help is public funding for nurses to retrain in the new systems, paid time to do it, and a rule that every ward keeps a safe number of real nurses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about money for training. Nobody should have to choose between learning the new tools and paying the rent, but that's exactly what a junior nurse on my pay does. If the course costs a month's rent, it doesn't matter how keen I am.

headlineQuote: Nobody should have to choose between learning the new tools and paying the rent, but that's exactly what a junior nurse on my pay does.
portrait: A **27-year-old** junior nurse on a respiratory ward who uses **AI tools** every day.
She lives alone in a studio where **rent** eats half her pay, with three weeks saved.
She wants to be the ward's **digital champion**, but knows her patient skills lag.
She moves from **uneasy** in most pictures to **anxious** at two years and **calm** at ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she couldn't keep up and might leave her **dad**.
whatWouldHelp: **Public funding** and paid time to retrain, plus safe nurse numbers on every ward.
